#1
L: On the field of dharma, on the field of the Kurus, assembled, wanting-to-fight — my people and the sons of Pāṇḍu too — what did they do, Sañjaya?
I: On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered and eager for battle, what did my sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu do, Sañjaya?
N: The whole poem is framed as a report: the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks his minister Sañjaya, who has been granted sight of the distant battlefield, and everything that follows is Sañjaya's answer. Two things to notice on the first line. First, sandhi: पाण्डवाश्चैव looks like one word but is three — pāṇḍavāḥ + ca + eva, the final -ḥ turning to -ś before c-, and ca + eva fusing to caiva. You will see this fusing on nearly every line; the reading under each word shows the words unfused. Second, the opening compound dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre: Kurukṣetra is a real place north of Delhi, and the poet sets 'field of dharma' beside it — the battle is over what is right. Māmakāḥ, 'mine', is the king's word for his own hundred sons.
#2
L: Having seen, then, the Pāṇḍava-army drawn-up, Duryodhana then, the teacher having-approached, the king spoke a word.
I: Sañjaya said: When he saw the Pāṇḍava army drawn up in battle order, King Duryodhana went up to his teacher and spoke.
N: Sanskrit narrative runs on gerunds — dṛṣṭvā 'having seen', upasaṃgamya 'having approached' — chained before a single finite verb, abravīt 'he spoke'. Read them as 'he saw ..., went up ..., and spoke'. The teacher is Droṇa, who taught the princes of both houses to fight. Vyūḍha, 'arrayed', is the technical word for an army in formation.
#3
L: Behold this of-the-sons-of-Pāṇḍu, O teacher, great army, drawn-up by the son of Drupada, by your pupil, the wise one.
I: 'Look, teacher, at this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, drawn up by Drupada's son, your own clever pupil.'
N: Paśyaitām is paśya + etām: the imperative 'look!' fused with 'this'. The jab is in the last line: Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who arrayed the enemy, was Droṇa's pupil — and Drupada, his father, was Droṇa's old enemy. Duryodhana is needling his teacher. Note the four words that agree with camūm 'army' (feminine accusative): etām, mahatīm, vyūḍhām — Sanskrit lets them scatter across the verse, and the endings tie them together.
#4
L: Here are heroes, great-bowmen, to Bhīma and Arjuna equal in battle: Yuyudhāna and Virāṭa and Drupada the great-chariot-warrior.
I: 'Here are heroes, mighty archers, a match for Bhīma and Arjuna in battle: Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada the great warrior.
N: The muster roll begins. Sanskrit strings names with ca ... ca, 'and ... and', where English uses one 'and'. Maheṣvāsa is mahā + iṣvāsa, 'great bow' used for the man who draws it. Mahāratha, literally 'great chariot', is a rank: a warrior able to fight ten thousand at once. The reading shows sandhi across the join: mahā + iṣvāsa gives maheṣvāsa, ā + i fusing to e.
#5
L: Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the king of Kāśī the valorous; Purujit and Kuntibhoja and Śaibya, bull-among-men.
I: 'Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna and the valiant king of Kāśī; Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Śaibya, a bull among men.
N: A verse of names, which is what the whole first half of this chapter is. Narapuṅgava, 'man-bull', is a standing compliment: the bull is the best of the herd. Vīryavān, 'possessing vīrya' (manly force), is the -vat suffix you will meet constantly — 'having X'.
#6
L: Yudhāmanyu the valiant, and Uttamaujas the valorous; the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī, all indeed great-chariot-warriors.
I: 'Bold Yudhāmanyu, valiant Uttamaujas, Subhadrā's son and the sons of Draupadī — every one of them a great warrior.
N: Names formed from mothers: Saubhadra 'son of Subhadrā' is Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son; the Draupadeyas are the five sons of Draupadī, one by each of the five Pāṇḍava brothers, to whom she was jointly married. Vikrānta uttamaujāḥ: the final -ḥ of vikrāntaḥ simply drops before the vowel u-, so the written form is विक्रान्त with no visarga.
#7
L: But of ours the distinguished ones, who [they are], take-note, O best of the twice-born; the leaders of my army, for information I name them to you.
I: 'But now take note, best of brahmins, of the outstanding men on our side, the leaders of my army; I name them so that you know them.
N: Dvijottama, 'best of the twice-born', addresses Droṇa as a brahmin — a brahmin who fights, which the poem does not remark on but the tradition did. The verse is built on a relative pair: ye ... tān, 'who ... them': 'those who are distinguished, take note of them'. Saṃjñārtham is an adverbial accusative, 'for the purpose of recognition'.
#8
L: Your honour, and Bhīṣma, and Karṇa, and Kṛpa victorious-in-battle; Aśvatthāman and Vikarṇa and the son of Somadatta likewise.
I: 'Yourself, and Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and Kṛpa who always wins his fights; Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and Somadatta's son too.
N: Bhavān is the polite 'you' — grammatically third person ('your honour'), so it takes a third-person verb. Karṇa is the tragic figure of the epic: Kuntī's first son, born before her marriage and abandoned, so the Pāṇḍavas' elder brother without their knowing it. The text here follows the usual (Śaṅkara) reading saumadattis tathaiva ca; some editions, including the GRETIL e-text collated for this file, read saumadattir jayadrathaḥ, 'Saumadatti and Jayadratha', instead.
#9
L: And other many heroes, for my sake having-given-up-their-lives, with-various-weapons-striking, all in-battle-skilled.
I: 'And many other heroes ready to lay down their lives for me, armed with weapons of every kind, all of them expert in war.
N: Three long compounds, each an adjective describing the heroes: tyakta-jīvitāḥ 'whose lives are given up' (a bahuvrīhi, the 'having-X' type of compound), nānā-śastra-praharaṇāḥ 'having various weapons as their means of striking', yuddha-viśāradāḥ 'battle-skilled'. Reading a Sanskrit compound means finding its last member (the head) and reading backwards.
#10
L: Insufficient is that army of ours, by Bhīṣma guarded; sufficient however is this army of theirs, by Bhīma guarded.
I: 'Our army, with Bhīṣma at its head, is not enough; theirs, with Bhīma at its head, is enough.
N: A famous ambiguity. Aparyāpta means 'not sufficient', and paryāpta 'sufficient' — read that way, Duryodhana is confessing weakness. But aparyāpta can also mean 'unlimited' and paryāpta 'limited', which gives the boast most commentators prefer: 'our army is unlimited, theirs is limited'. The verse pairs Bhīṣma and Bhīma, the two great champions, in matching half-lines, and the poem itself does not settle which reading is right; the literal layer above gives the plain dictionary sense.
#11
L: And in all the positions, each-at-his-post standing, Bhīṣma alone let-them-guard, your honours, all indeed.
I: 'So let all of you, each holding his own post in every part of the line, guard Bhīṣma above all.'
N: Bhīṣmam evābhirakṣantu: eva 'alone, above all' is the stress-word of the verse, and eva + abhirakṣantu fuse to evābhirakṣantu. Abhirakṣantu is a third-person imperative, 'let them guard'; with bhavantaḥ ('your honours', the polite plural) it works as a courteous command. Ayana is literally a 'going', here the gaps or stations of the battle-line.
#12
L: Of him producing joy, the Kuru-elder, the grandsire, a lion-roar having-roared aloud, a conch blew, the majestic one.
I: Then the grandsire, the old man of the Kurus, to cheer Duryodhana, roared like a lion and blew his conch.
N: Tasya harṣaṃ saṃjanayan, 'producing joy of him', i.e. to hearten Duryodhana, whom the speech has just betrayed as anxious. The grandsire is Bhīṣma, called pitāmaha 'grandfather' though strictly a grand-uncle. The conch (śaṅkha) is the war-trumpet of the epic; the next verses are a catalogue of them. Dadhmau is the perfect of dhmā 'to blow' — reduplicated, like Greek or Latin perfects.
#13
L: Then conches and kettledrums and tabors, drums and horns suddenly were sounded; that sound tumultuous was.
I: Then conches, kettledrums, tabors, big drums and horns all at once were sounded, and the noise was tremendous.
N: The last three words are a sandhi exercise: śabdastumulo'bhavat is śabdaḥ + tumulaḥ + abhavat. The first -aḥ becomes -as before t-; the second becomes -o before a-, and the a- of abhavat then vanishes, its absence marked in Devanagari by the sign ऽ (avagraha), which the transliteration shows as an apostrophe. Abhyahanyanta is a passive, 'were struck': drums are 'struck' even when they are blown.
#14
L: Then, with white horses yoked, in a great chariot standing, Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava too their divine conches blew, the two.
I: Then, standing in a great chariot yoked with white horses, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna blew their divine conches.
N: Sanskrit has a dual number for exactly two: sthitau 'the two standing', divyau śaṅkhau 'the two divine conches', pradadhmatuḥ 'the two blew'. Mādhava (descendant of Madhu) is Kṛṣṇa; 'the Pāṇḍava' here is Arjuna, whose chariot Kṛṣṇa drives. Note the locative absolute: śvetair hayair yukte ... syandane sthitau, 'standing in a chariot yoked with white horses'.
#15
L: Pāñcajanya the Lord-of-the-senses, Devadatta the Winner-of-wealth; Pauṇḍra blew, the great conch, the one-of-terrible-deeds, Wolf-belly.
I: Kṛṣṇa blew Pāñcajanya, Arjuna blew Devadatta, and Bhīma of the terrible deeds, the Wolf-belly, blew his great conch Pauṇḍra.
N: Every name here is an epithet, and the poem uses them the way Homer uses 'swift-footed': Hṛṣīkeśa 'lord of the senses' is Kṛṣṇa, Dhanañjaya 'winner of wealth' is Arjuna, Vṛkodara 'wolf-belly' is Bhīma, famous for his appetite. The one verb dadhmau serves all three clauses. The conches have names too, as swords do in Beowulf.
#16
L: Anantavijaya the king, Kuntī's-son Yudhiṣṭhira; Nakula and Sahadeva Sughoṣa-and-Maṇipuṣpaka.
I: King Yudhiṣṭhira, Kuntī's son, blew Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka.
N: The verb is carried over from verse 15 — no verb appears here at all. Sughoṣa-maṇipuṣpakau is a dvandva, a pair-compound, in the dual: 'Sughoṣa-and-Maṇipuṣpaka', one conch each for the twins. Yudhiṣṭhira is 'the king' (rājā) because he is the eldest Pāṇḍava and the rightful heir.
#17
L: And the Kāśī-king, supreme-archer, and Śikhaṇḍin the great-chariot-warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Virāṭa and Sātyaki the unconquered,
I: And the king of Kāśī, a supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍin the great warrior, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa and Sātyaki the unconquered,
N: Verses 17 and 18 are one sentence; the verb comes at the end of 18. Śikhaṇḍin has the strangest story on the field: born a daughter of Drupada, raised as a son, and later made male by a spirit's gift — Bhīṣma will refuse to fight him, and that refusal is how Bhīṣma falls. Sātyaki is the same man as Yuyudhāna in verse 4.
#18
L: Drupada and the sons of Draupadī all-together, O lord of the earth, and the son of Subhadrā the mighty-armed — the conches they blew, each-his-own.
I: and Drupada and the sons of Draupadī, O lord of the earth, and Subhadrā's mighty-armed son, each blew his own conch.
N: Pṛthivīpate, 'lord of the earth', is Sañjaya addressing the blind king — a reminder that all of this is being reported to him. Pṛthak pṛthak, 'separately, separately', is the Sanskrit way of saying 'each his own'; doubling a word for distribution is common. Dadhmuḥ is the plural of the perfect: 'they blew'.
#19
L: That din of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra the hearts tore-apart, sky and earth too, tumultuous, making-resound.
I: That din, resounding through sky and earth, tore the hearts of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons.
N: Dhārtarāṣṭra, 'son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra', is the poem's word for the Kaurava side, and the king hearing this is Dhṛtarāṣṭra himself. Vyadārayat is a causative, 'caused to split'; vyanunādayan, a causative participle, 'making [sky and earth] resound' — the -aya- in each is the causative mark. Nabhaś ca: nabhaḥ + ca, the visarga turning to ś before c.
#20
L: Then, arrayed having-seen the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Monkey-bannered one, as the weapon-clash was beginning, his bow having-raised, the Pāṇḍava
I: Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up for battle, and the clash of weapons about to begin, Arjuna of the monkey banner raised his bow
N: Verses 20 and 21 are one sentence: the subject 'the Pāṇḍava' (Arjuna) is introduced here and does his speaking in the next verse. Kapidhvaja, 'monkey-bannered': the monkey-god Hanumān sits on Arjuna's flag. Pravṛtte śastrasaṃpāte is a locative absolute, 'the weapon-clash having begun' — the absolute construction, two locatives together, serves as a whole clause of time.
#21
L: to the Lord-of-the-senses then this word said, O lord of the earth: 'Between the two armies, in the middle, my chariot halt, O Unshakeable one.
I: and said this to Kṛṣṇa, O lord of the earth: 'Halt my chariot between the two armies, Acyuta,
N: The finite verb of verses 20–21 is āha, 'he said'. Senayor ubhayor madhye — 'in the middle of both armies' — is repeated word for word in verse 24, when Kṛṣṇa does it. Sthāpaya is the causative imperative of sthā 'stand': 'make [it] stand', i.e. halt. Me 'cyuta: me + acyuta, with the avagraha marking the swallowed a-.
#22
L: until I survey these, wanting-to-fight, standing-arrayed — with whom by me together it-must-be-fought in this battle-enterprise.
I: so that I can look over these men standing here eager for battle, and see whom I must fight in this great undertaking.
N: Yoddhavyam is a gerundive, 'is to be fought', used impersonally: 'fighting must be done by me' (mayā) 'together with whom' (kaiḥ saha) — the Sanskrit passive-impersonal where English says 'whom I must fight'. Nirīkṣe is a middle-voice form, 'I look over for myself'. The Wikisource text prints निरिक्षे with a short i, a misprint; the verb is nir-īkṣ with long ī, as in the GRETIL text, and the long vowel is printed here.
#23
L: Those-about-to-fight I look-at, who these here are-assembled, of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, the evil-minded, in battle wishing-to-do-a-favour.'
I: Let me see who has come here to fight, eager to please the wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle.'
N: Ya ete 'tra: the relative ye 'who' loses its final -e's independence before a vowel and is written य; ete + atra gives ete 'tra with avagraha. Dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbuddheḥ, 'of the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra', is Duryodhana in the singular. Priyacikīrṣavaḥ is a desiderative adjective — cikīrṣu 'wishing to do', from kṛ — the same formation as yuyutsu 'wishing to fight' in verse 1.
#24
L: Thus addressed, the Lord-of-the-senses by the Thick-haired one, O Bhārata, between the two armies in the middle having-halted the best-of-chariots,
I: Sañjaya said: Addressed in this way by Arjuna, O Bhārata, Kṛṣṇa halted that finest of chariots between the two armies,
N: Guḍākeśa, an epithet of Arjuna, is explained two ways by the tradition: 'thick-haired' or 'conqueror of sleep' (guḍākā). Bhārata, 'descendant of Bharata', is Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the same title is later given to Arjuna, since both houses descend from Bharata. Verses 24–25 are one sentence, ending in uvāca 'he said'.
#25
L: in front of Bhīṣma and Droṇa and of all the rulers-of-the-earth, said: 'O son of Pṛthā, behold these assembled Kurus' — thus.
I: facing Bhīṣma, Droṇa and all the kings, and said: 'Arjuna, behold these Kurus gathered here.'
N: Iti at the end marks the close of a quotation — Sanskrit's closing quotation mark, placed after the words spoken. Note that Kṛṣṇa says kurūn, 'Kurus': both armies are Kurus, descendants of Kuru, and the word quietly makes Arjuna's point for him before he makes it. Pārtha, 'son of Pṛthā' (another name of Kuntī), is Kṛṣṇa's usual address to Arjuna.
#26
L: There saw, standing, the son of Pṛthā fathers and grandfathers, teachers, maternal-uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends likewise,
I: There Arjuna saw, standing in their ranks, fathers and grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends,
N: The second line is one unbroken Devanagari string — ācāryānmātulānbhrātṝnputrānpautrānsakhīṃstathā — because each accusative plural ends in a consonant (-n) and Sanskrit writes a consonant-final word joined to the next. The reading under it separates the seven words. Pitṝn 'fathers' means the father's generation — uncles like Bhīṣma's kin, not Arjuna's own father Pāṇḍu, who is dead. Sakhīṃs tathā: the final -n of sakhīn becomes -ṃs before t-.
#27
L: fathers-in-law and friends too, in both the armies alike. Them having-surveyed, he, Kuntī's son, all the kinsmen standing-arrayed,
I: fathers-in-law and friends as well, in both armies alike. When Kuntī's son had looked over all those kinsmen standing there,
N: Ubhayor api — 'in both, even': the point of the whole list is that the same kinds of kin stand on both sides. Verses 27–28 form one sentence: the gerund samīkṣya 'having surveyed' here, the finite verb abravīt 'he spoke' in the next verse. Kaunteya 'son of Kuntī' is a third way of naming Arjuna by his mother (with Pārtha).
#28
L: by pity supreme overcome, despairing, this he spoke: 'Having seen this own-people, Kṛṣṇa, wanting-to-fight, drawn-up,
I: he was overcome by deep pity and said in despair: 'Krishna, seeing my own people here, drawn up and eager for battle,
N: Kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ: 'entered by supreme pity' — āviṣṭa, from ā-viś 'enter', is the word for being possessed, as by a spirit; the emotion takes Arjuna over. Viṣīdan 'sinking, despairing' gives the chapter its traditional title, Arjuna-viṣāda-yoga, 'the yoga of Arjuna's despair'. Svajana, 'own-people', is the key word of the chapter: not 'the enemy' but 'my own'. The BORI critical text reads the plural here, dṛṣṭvemān svajanān ... yuyutsūn samavasthitān, 'seeing these kinsmen of mine drawn up'; the vulgate's singular svajanam is a collective.
#29
L: sink my limbs, and the mouth dries-up, and trembling in my body and hair-bristling arises.
I: my limbs give way, my mouth goes dry, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.
N: The symptoms of shock, listed with present-tense verbs: sīdanti 'they sink', pariśuṣyati 'it dries up', jāyate 'it arises'. Mama and me are both 'my' — mama the full form, me the short enclitic that cannot stand first in a clause. Romaharṣa, 'hair-thrill', is horripilation, the hair standing on end; in Sanskrit poetry it can be a sign of joy as easily as of dread.
#30
L: Gāṇḍīva slips from the hand, and the skin too burns-all-over; and I cannot stand, and reels, as it were, my mind.
I: Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand, my skin is burning all over; I cannot stay on my feet, and my mind seems to reel.
N: Gāṇḍīva is Arjuna's bow, a named weapon like a sword in Beowulf. Śaknomy avasthātum: śaknomi 'I am able' + the infinitive; -i before a vowel becomes -y, which is why the written form is शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं. Bhramatīva is bhramati + iva, 'reels as it were' — iva, 'like, as if', is the poet's constant softener.
#31
L: And I see omens contrary, O Keśava, and I do not foresee good, having killed own-people in battle.
I: I see evil omens, Keśava, and I can see no good coming from killing my own people in battle.
N: Śreyo 'nupaśyāmi: śreyaḥ + anupaśyāmi, -aḥ becoming -o before a- and the a- dropping (avagraha). Śreyas, 'the better thing, welfare', is one of the Gītā's central words; the next chapter turns on it. Hatvā, 'having killed', is the gerund of han — the same root gives hantum 'to kill' in verse 35 and ghnataḥ 'killing' in the same verse.
#32
L: I do not desire victory, Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom and pleasures. What to us with a kingdom, Govinda, what with enjoyments or with life?
I: I have no wish for victory, Kṛṣṇa, nor for a kingdom and its pleasures. What good is a kingdom to us, Govinda — what good are pleasures, or life itself?
N: Kiṃ naḥ rājyena — 'what [is there] to us by a kingdom?' — is the Sanskrit idiom for 'what use is a kingdom to us?': kim with a dative of the person and an instrumental of the thing. Govinda, 'finder of cows', recalls Kṛṣṇa's youth as a cowherd. The verse has four ca's and one vā ('or'); Sanskrit likes to mark each item.
#33
L: For whose sake is desired by us the kingdom, enjoyments and pleasures — they, these, stand-arrayed in battle, their lives having-given-up, and their wealth.
I: The very people for whose sake we wanted a kingdom, enjoyment and pleasure are standing here in battle, ready to give up their lives and their wealth.
N: Yeṣām ... te: the relative-correlative frame again, 'of whom ... they'. Kāṅkṣitam is a past participle used as the predicate, 'is desired', with the agent in the enclitic naḥ 'by us'. Ta ime 'vasthitāḥ: te loses the -e's independence before a vowel (written त), and ime + avasthitāḥ fuse with the avagraha.
#34
L: Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers, maternal-uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and kinsmen likewise.
I: Teachers, fathers, sons and grandfathers, uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and kinsmen —
N: The same kin-list as verse 26, now in the nominative, as the subject of the sentence that runs through verse 35: these are the ones Arjuna will not kill. Two words are new: śyāla 'wife's brother' and saṃbandhin 'relative by marriage'. Putrās tathaiva: putrāḥ + tathā + eva, with -āḥ becoming -ās before t-. BORI spells syālāḥ for śyālāḥ, a spelling variant of the same word.
#35
L: These I do not wish to kill, even though they are killing, O slayer of Madhu — even for the sake of the kingship of the three worlds; how much less for the sake of the earth!
I: I do not want to kill them, Madhusūdana, even if they kill me — not for the sake of ruling all three worlds, let alone for the sake of the earth.
N: Ghnato 'pi — 'even [them] killing', i.e. even if they are the ones doing the killing: a participle in the accusative agreeing with etān. Api ... kiṃ nu: 'even for X; how much less for Y' — a standard Sanskrit escalation. Trailokya is the triple world of Vedic cosmology (earth, air, heaven); Madhusūdana names Kṛṣṇa as the god who slew the demon Madhu.
#36
L: Having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, for us what joy would there be, O Janārdana? Evil alone would cling to us, having killed these aggressors.
I: What joy could we have, Janārdana, in killing Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons? Only sin would come to us if we killed them, aggressors though they are.
N: The second line is one unbroken string of eight words in the Devanagari — see the reading. Ātatāyin, 'one who comes with bow drawn', is a legal term: an aggressor whom the law-books allow one to kill without guilt. Arjuna grants the point (they are ātatāyinaḥ) and rejects the permission. Syāj janārdana: syāt + janārdana, -t assimilating to the following j-.
#37
L: Therefore we are not entitled to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen; for our own people having killed, how could we be happy, O Mādhava?
I: So it is not right for us to kill Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons, our own relations. How could we be happy, Mādhava, after killing our own people?
N: Nārhāḥ is na + arhāḥ, 'not entitled, not right': arha with an infinitive (hantum) is how Sanskrit says 'ought to'. Syāma is the optative, 'we might be' — the mood of what could or should happen, which the whole speech is written in. Svabāndhavān and svajanam: the prefix sva- 'own' twice in one verse. BORI reads sabāndhavān, 'together with their kinsmen', where the vulgate's svabāndhavān makes the Kauravas themselves 'our own kinsmen'.
#38
L: Even if these do not see, their-minds-ruined-by-greed, the fault caused-by-the-ruin-of-the-family and the crime in treachery-to-friends,
I: Even if these men, their judgement ruined by greed, cannot see the evil in destroying a family or the crime of betraying friends,
N: Yady apy ete is yadi + api + ete: two final -i's become -y before vowels. Lobhopahatacetasaḥ is a bahuvrīhi describing ete: 'whose minds (cetas) are struck (upahata) by greed (lobha)'. The verse is the 'if' half of a sentence completed in 39.
#39
L: how should it not be known by us, from this evil to turn back — the fault caused-by-the-ruin-of-the-family clearly-seeing, O Janārdana?
I: how can we, who see clearly the evil in destroying a family, not know enough to turn back from this sin, Janārdana?
N: Jñeyam asmābhiḥ — 'to be known by us' — the gerundive again, as in verse 22, with the agent in the instrumental. Prapaśyadbhiḥ 'by [us] seeing clearly' agrees with asmābhiḥ. Pāpād asmān nivartitum: the ablative 'from this sin' with the infinitive 'to turn back'; note -t + a- → -d a- and -t + n- → -n n- in the written string.
#40
L: In the ruin of the family perish the family-laws, the eternal ones; when the law has perished, the whole family lawlessness overpowers too.
I: When a family is destroyed, its age-old laws perish; and when the law is gone, lawlessness overwhelms the whole family.
N: Dharma here is the concrete kula-dharma, the customs and duties of a particular family, not an abstraction. Dharme naṣṭe is a locative absolute, 'the dharma being lost'. Kṛtsnam adharmo 'bhibhavaty uta: four words fused in the writing — adharmaḥ + abhibhavati gives adharmo 'bhi-, and -ti + uta gives -ty uta.
#41
L: From the overpowering of lawlessness, Kṛṣṇa, are corrupted the women of the family; when the women are corrupted, O Vārṣṇeya, arises class-confusion.
I: When lawlessness prevails, Kṛṣṇa, the women of the family are corrupted; and when the women are corrupted, Vārṣṇeya, the classes become mixed.
N: Arjuna's argument now runs as a chain of causes, each verse taking the last word of the previous as its starting point (adharma → adharmābhibhavāt). Strīṣu duṣṭāsu is a locative absolute, 'the women being corrupted'. Varṇasaṃkara, 'mixing of the varṇas' (the four social classes), was the classical Indian nightmare of social collapse. Vārṣṇeya: Kṛṣṇa as a member of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
#42
L: Confusion is for hell alone, of the family-destroyers and of the family; for fall their ancestors, their rice-ball-and-water-rites cut off.
I: That mixing leads straight to hell, both for the family's destroyers and for the family itself; for their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice and water.
N: The ancestors (pitaraḥ, the 'fathers') depend on their descendants' offerings: the piṇḍa, a ball of cooked rice, and udaka, water, offered at the śrāddha rite. Without living heirs of pure line to perform them, the dead 'fall' from their place. Luptapiṇḍodakakriyāḥ is a four-member bahuvrīhi: 'whose piṇḍa-and-water-rites are cut off'. Narakāyaiva: narakāya + eva.
#43
L: By these faults of the family-destroyers, which-cause-class-confusion, are abolished the caste-laws and the family-laws, the everlasting ones.
I: Through these sins of the family's destroyers, which throw the classes into confusion, the everlasting laws of caste and family are wiped out.
N: The whole first line is instrumental — 'by these faults ... of the destroyers ... causing confusion' — and the second line gives the passive verb and its subject: utsādyante 'are abolished', jātidharmāḥ kuladharmāś ca. Jāti, 'birth-group', is the narrower unit within the broad varṇa. Kuladharmāś ca: -āḥ + ca → -āś ca.
#44
L: Of men whose-family-laws-are-destroyed, O Janārdana, in hell for-an-indefinite-time a dwelling comes to be — thus we have heard.
I: Men whose family laws have been destroyed, Janārdana, must dwell in hell for an unending time — so we have heard it told.
N: Anuśuśruma, 'we have heard by tradition', is a perfect of śru 'hear' with anu-, the verb for received teaching; Arjuna is citing what he was taught, not his own view. The text follows the reading narake 'niyatam, 'in hell, for an indefinite time' (aniyatam), the reading Śaṅkara's commentary explains; many printed editions read narake niyatam, 'in hell, certainly', which the GRETIL e-text also has. Bhavatīty anuśuśruma: bhavati + iti + anuśuśruma, with -i + i- → -ī- and -i + a- → -y a-.
#45
L: Ah, alas! a great evil to do we have resolved — we who, out of greed for the pleasures of kingship, to kill our own people are bent.
I: Alas, what a great sin we have set our minds to — ready to kill our own kin out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom!
N: Aho bata: two exclamations of dismay, one after the other. Vyavasitā vayam, 'we are resolved' — the perfect participle used as a past tense with the pronoun, a construction Sanskrit uses constantly instead of a finite verb. Yad here means 'in that, seeing that', introducing the reason for the dismay.
#46
L: If me, unresisting, unarmed, the weapon-in-hand sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle should kill, that for me safer would be.
I: If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, weapons in hand, were to kill me in battle, unarmed and unresisting, that would be better for me.
N: Two bahuvrīhis frame the verse: apratīkāram aśastram 'without resistance, without weapon' (Arjuna, accusative) against śastrapāṇayaḥ 'weapon-in-hand' (the Kauravas, nominative). Hanyuḥ is optative, 'should they kill'; bhavet, 'it would be' — the if-clause and its result both in the optative. Kṣemataram: the comparative -tara, 'more kṣema', more to my welfare.
#47
L: Thus having spoken, Arjuna, in the battle, on the chariot-seat sat down, having cast aside the arrow-and-bow, his-mind-shaken-with-grief.
I: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus, in the midst of the battle Arjuna sank down on the seat of his chariot and let fall his bow and arrow, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
N: The narrator's voice returns for one verse. Rathopastha upāviśat: ratha + upastha gives rathopastha-, and the locative -e stays unchanged before the vowel u-, which is why it is written रथोपस्थ with no ending visible. Saśaraṃ cāpam, 'the bow with its arrow' — sa- 'with' prefixed to śara. The chapter ends on a bahuvrīhi, śoka-saṃvigna-mānasaḥ, 'whose mind is shaken by grief', and the teaching begins in chapter 2.
